quotes: Ancient Mesopotamia—in the Fertile Crescent of the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers—boasted the most advanced and most powerful culture in the Mediterranean region for more than a millennium. The cultural dominance of ancient Mesopotamia has a lot to do with Mesopotamians’ development of the first writing system in the world—cuneiform—which survives today on clay tablets that date from about 3000 BCE to about 100 CE.

Don’t get me wrong; Mesopotamian rulers had been primarily kings for a long time already, but with the theological rise of Marduk, there was a correlative rise in patriarchal governmental structures, as well as a correlative collapse in the status, autonomy, and power of women.

Lamashtu is a demoness, and she is the daughter of a god; she is thus immortal, but not fully divine. Unlike other Mesopotamian demons, who can only act on the orders of the greater gods, Lamashtu can act entirely on her own. She is an autonomous demon.

all this very real and very abject terror about reproduction got rolled up into and personified by Lamashtu, demoness of the night, drinker of blood, eater of flesh, slayer of children, untimely opener of wombs, ravager of women.

First, we learn that Lamashtu is highborn, the daughter of Anu, one of the most powerful and ancient gods in the Mesopotamian pantheon. Second, we learn that her “malevolent will” and “base counsel” caused her father, Anu, to banish her from heaven.

Let me slow this down for a moment, because the point is crucial: This is an origin myth in which a female deity is literally demonized for speaking out in a way that offended Patriarchy. The result of her speaking out is to spread reproductive violence across the human world.
It was her father who loosed Lamashtu on the world. Patriarchy made her; Patriarchy sicced her on the world of human women, children, babies, and fetuses.

This strange duality, wherein Lamashtu is both repulsively doglike and somehow weirdly alluring, is one we’ll see play itself out again and again for the next several thousand years: Monstrous Bitches are almost always both sexy and repulsive.

Fierce, wicked, sneaky, and unnatural, Lamashtu has the power to prevent cervical dilation in a laboring woman; any reader who has endured labor will shudder in empathy at such a power. And remember, this is the ancient world, which lacked anesthetics and dilation-producing drugs. A woman in labor in the ancient world whose cervix wouldn’t dilate would simply die, as would her baby.

Over a thousand years after the earliest incantations to Lamashtu, probably somewhere around the year 1100 BCE, Mesopotamian culture produced an epic poem on a set of seven clay tablets. Enuma Elish is a creation myth in three parts: the creation of the gods, the creation of the world, and the creation of man.

Tiamat has a second power, one at least as frightening as her womb, and it’s a power she shares with Lamashtu: her voice. Specifically, Tiamat has the ability to recite incantations—to spellcast—in a way that no one else can even respond to, let alone combat. Her voice is a paralytic agent, which stuns her male assailants into silence and abject fear.

Symbolically, her swelling belly represents Marduk’s hostile takeover of her reproductive power, and Marduk’s sharp arrow represents his penetrating her. Symbolically, then, Marduk rapes Tiamat to death.

Tiamat was scary in theory, but Lamashtu was scary in practice. Tiamat was scary in the past; Lamashtu was scary in the present. Lamashtu was never defeated, because she could never be defeated; she could only temporarily be warded off.

But there is a crucial difference between them: Tiamat must die, whereas Lamashtu must be placated or conjured into leaving—at least temporarily—the house she appears to be menacing. Scourge of babies, scourge of women, scourge of children, all in a way that Tiamat had not been.

Sex, reproduction, and voice—not coincidentally the very same things that are battlegrounds for women’s political status in popular culture today. Women have been laboring under the burden of demonization for their sexuality, their reproductive agency, and their voices for thousands of years. Because ultimately, however terrifying and however female she is, the Monstrous Bitch is an ideological tool that serves the Patriarchy—indeed, the monstrosity of both Lamashtu and Tiamat is created by the Patriarchy—and it has relied on her and on her demonization for as long as the world has had writing.
